# 6.1 Update Scope & Execution Methods

> "updateOne(filter, update) updates the first document that matches a query filter, using update operators such as $set to modify specific fields without replacing the whole document. updateMany(filter, update) updates every document that matches a query filter, applying the same update operators to each matching document."

## 1. Storage Engine & Wire Protocol Architecture

At the wire protocol layer, `updateOne(filter, update)` and `updateMany(filter, update)` dispatch `{ update: "<col>", updates: [ { q: <filter>, u: <update>, multi: false | true } ] }`. Under WiredTiger, each matched document is mutated atomically in place under an exclusive document-level latch without replacing unreferenced BSON fields.

From a systems engineering perspective within **6. Field Modification & In-Place Update Operators (CRUD Update)**, sub-topic `6.1` defines critical invariants across the `OP_MSG` wire protocol, WiredTiger storage extents (`collection-*.wt`, `index-*.wt`), and BSON memory buffers.

## 2. Exhaustive L-3 & L-4 Leaf Specification Analysis

### 2.1 L-3.1 Single-Target (`updateOne`, `multi: false`) vs. Multi-Target (`updateMany`, `multi: true`)

`updateOne()` halts its index/collection scan immediately after acquiring a write latch and applying `<update>` to the first matching document (`matchedCount: 0 | 1`). `updateMany()` sweeps across all matching documents (`matchedCount: N`), applying `<update>` atomically to each document in sequence.

### 2.2 L-3.2 Operator Mandate vs. Full-Document Replacement & Return Telemetry

Both `updateOne()` and `updateMany()` enforce a strict syntactic check: every top-level key in the second `<update>` argument must start with `$` (such as `$set`, `$inc`, `$push`, `$pull`); passing an un-prefixed object like `{ age: 20 }` throws `MongoInvalidArgumentError: Update document requires atomic operators`. Furthermore, if a matched document already holds the exact target value (`age: 20`), WiredTiger skips the redundant write (`matchedCount: 1, modifiedCount: 0`).

## 3. Systems-Level `mongosh` Implementation & Edge-Case Verification

The production-grade `mongosh` script below exercises the underlying wire protocol semantics, storage engine invariants, and edge-case boundary conditions for this sub-topic.

```javascript
// 1. Single-target in-place mutation (wire flag multi: false)
db.students.updateOne(
  { name: "Rahul" },
  { $set: { age: 20 } }
);

// 2. Multi-target batch mutation (wire flag multi: true)
db.students.updateMany(
  { age: 18 },
  { $set: { promoted: true } }
);

// 3. Upsert option: insert document if matchedCount === 0
db.students.updateOne(
  { name: "Vikram" },
  { $set: { age: 19, grade: 9 } },
  { upsert: true }
);
```

In high-throughput production deployments, verifying how each `mongosh` command translates into `OP_MSG` frames, B-tree index scans, and WiredTiger locks is essential for predictable latency.

## 4. Complete Architectural Subtree & State Diagram

The full-depth architectural diagram below formalizes the state transitions, wire RPCs, and L-3/L-4 leaf specifications governing this sub-topic.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Client as mongosh
    participant WT as mongod (WiredTiger)
    Client->>WT: updateMany({ age: 18 }, { $set: { promoted: true } })
    loop For each matching document (multi: true)
        WT->>WT: Acquire document latch & mutate BSON field in-place
        WT->>WT: Update affected secondary indexes & append oplog
    end
    WT-->>Client: { acknowledged: true, matchedCount: k, modifiedCount: k }
```

Every branch in the diagram corresponds directly to an enforceable server invariant inside `mongod`.

## 5. Systems Trade-Off Matrix & High-Difficulty Exam Traps

| Architectural Property | `updateOne(filter, update, opts)` | `updateMany(filter, update, opts)` |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Wire Protocol Flag | `multi: false` | `multi: true` |
| Concurrency Latch Scope | Single document exclusive latch | Per-document latch acquired sequentially |
| No-Op Write Suppression | `modifiedCount: 0` if value unchanged | Increments `modifiedCount` only for changed docs |
| Empty Filter `{}` Behavior | Updates first document in natural order | Updates 100% of documents in collection |

### Key Exam Traps & Takeaways

- **Architectural Trap — `updateOne` vs. `replaceOne`**: `updateOne()` requires `$` operators and mutates fields in place, whereas `replaceOne()` forbids `$` operators and replaces the entire document (except `_id`).
- **Atomicity Boundary of `updateMany()`**: Each individual document inside `updateMany()` is updated atomically, but the multi-document batch as a whole can interleave with other operations unless executed inside a multi-document transaction.
- **Immutable `_id` Invariant**: Attempting `{ $set: { _id: 999 } }` inside `updateOne()` or `updateMany()` throws an immutable field error (`code: 66`).
